Appendix A Derivations

A.1 Derivation of LNP-Components

In this section, we provide a detailed derivation of the decomposition of loss dynamics into three components: the loss-network-position (LNP) decomposition. This framework enables computationally efficient calculation of the spectral position χpos\chi_{\text{pos}}, which typically would require expensive computations of the empirical neural tangent kernel (eNTK). While the main idea is presented in Section 3, we here provide a detailed derivation of the framework that includes dynamics of stochastic mini-batch training.

Let 𝐗=[𝐱1,…,𝐱D]T\mathbf{X}=[\mathbf{x}_{1},...,\mathbf{x}_{D}]^{T} denote the matrix of DD training inputs 𝐱i∈ℝn\mathbf{x}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} and 𝐘=[y1,…,yD]T\mathbf{Y}=[y_{1},...,y_{D}]^{T} be the corresponding matrix of targets 𝐲i∈ℝm\mathbf{y}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{m}, which can be either supervised labels or self-supervised targets. Let the neural network be represented by a function f⁡(𝐱,𝜽)∈ℝmf(\mathbf{x};\boldsymbol{\theta})\in\mathbb{R}^{m} with NN parameters 𝜽∈ℝN\boldsymbol{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^{N}.

The training process involves minimizing a loss function ℒ⁡(f⁡(𝐗,𝜽),𝐘)=:ℒ⁡(𝐗,𝜽)\mathcal{L}(f(\mathbf{X};\boldsymbol{\theta}),\mathbf{Y})=:\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{X},\boldsymbol{\theta}), over the dataset. For simplicity, we omit the explicit notation of targets, as each input has a corresponding pair. During training, the parameters 𝜽t\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t} at training step t∈ℕt\in\mathbb{N} are updated iteratively using stochastic gradient descent according to

Δ​𝜽t:=𝜽t+1−𝜽t=−η​∇𝜽ℒ​(𝐗t,𝜽t),\Delta\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t}:=\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t+1}-\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t}=-\eta\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{X}_{t},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t}), (13)

where η\eta is the learning rate and 𝐗t\mathbf{X}_{t} is the mini-batch of data sampled at training step tt. In each training step, the loss changes according to

Δ​ℒt:=ℒ⁡(𝐗t+1,𝜽t+1)−ℒ⁡(𝐗t,𝜽t),\Delta\mathcal{L}_{t}:=\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{X}_{t+1},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t+1})-\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{X}_{t},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t})\,, (14)

where the updated loss is typically evaluated on a new mini-batch 𝐗t+1\mathbf{X}_{t+1}. Analyzing the full non-linear dynamics of neural networks during training is challenging, which is why we will focus on the linear component of the loss change. That is, for small step sizes η\eta, we can linearize the loss change around the current parameters 𝜽t\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t}:

Δ​ℒt=∇𝜽T​ℒ​(𝐗t+1,𝜽t)​Δ​𝜽t⏟(linearized change)+O⁡(η2)⏟=:νt​(non-linear correction)=−η​∇𝜽Tℒ​(𝐗t+1,𝜽t)​∇𝜽ℒ​(𝐗t,𝜽t)+νt\begin{split}\Delta\mathcal{L}_{t}&=\underbrace{\nabla^{T}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{X}_{t+1},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t})\,\Delta\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t}}_{\text{(linearized change)}}+\underbrace{O\!\left(\eta^{2}\right)}_{=:\,\nu_{t}\,\text{(non-linear correction)}}\\ &=-\eta\,\nabla^{T}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{X}_{t+1},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t})\,\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{X}_{t},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t})+\nu_{t}\end{split} (15)

Note that the loss change is induced by the mini-batch 𝐗t\mathbf{X}_{t} sampled at step tt, while the loss is evaluated on a different mini-batch 𝐗t+1\mathbf{X}_{t+1} at step t+1t+1. This is an extension of the derivation provided in Section 3, where we assumed full-batch training for simplicity.

We will now focus on the linearized loss change term in Equation 15 and derive its LNP-decomposition. To do this, we first simplify the notation: we drop the explicit dependence of the parameters 𝜽t\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t} and abstract the mini-batches 𝐗t\mathbf{X}_{t} and 𝐗t+1\mathbf{X}_{t+1} as batches 𝐗A\mathbf{X}_{A} and 𝐗B\mathbf{X}_{B}, respectively. This allows us to express the linearized loss change more compactly as

δ​ℒ​(A,B):=∇𝜽TℒB​∇𝜽ℒA:=∇𝜽T​ℒ​(𝐗B,𝜽)​∇𝜽ℒ​(𝐗A,𝜽)\delta\mathcal{L}(A,B):=\nabla^{T}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}^{B}\,\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}^{A}:=\nabla^{T}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{X}_{B},\boldsymbol{\theta})\,\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{X}_{A},\boldsymbol{\theta}) (16)

We apply the chain rule to express the loss gradients with respect to the parameters 𝜽\boldsymbol{\theta} in terms of the network outputs ff. For batch AA, this reads

∇𝜽ℒA=(∇𝜽fA)T​∇fℒA,\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}^{A}=(\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}f^{A})^{T}\,\nabla_{f}\mathcal{L}^{A}\,, (17)

where ∇fℒ∈ℝm​|A|\nabla_{f}\mathcal{L}\in\mathbb{R}^{m|A|} is the loss gradient with respect to the network outputs and ∇𝜽f∈ℝN×m​|A|\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}f\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times m|A|} is the Jacobian of the network outputs with respect to the parameters evaluated on batch AA. |A||A| and |B||B| denote the batch sizes of batches AA and BB, respectively. Note that we have vectorized the network outputs over the batch dimension, such that fA=[f⁡(𝐱i,𝜽)]𝐱i∈𝐗A∈ℝm​|A|f^{A}=[f(\mathbf{x}_{i};\boldsymbol{\theta})]_{\mathbf{x}_{i}\in\mathbf{X}_{A}}\in\mathbb{R}^{m|A|} and ∇fℒA=[∇f⁡(𝐱i,𝜽)ℒ​(𝐗A,𝜽)]𝐱i∈𝐗A∈ℝm​|A|\nabla_{f}\mathcal{L}^{A}=[\nabla_{f(\mathbf{x}_{i};\boldsymbol{\theta})}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{X}_{A},\boldsymbol{\theta})]_{\mathbf{x}_{i}\in\mathbf{X}_{A}}\in\mathbb{R}^{m|A|}. Dataset BB is treated analogously. Inserting this into Equation 16, we obtain

δ​ℒ​(A,B)\displaystyle\delta\mathcal{L}(A,B) =(∇fℒB)T∇𝜽fB​(∇𝜽fA)T⏟=:ΘA​B∇fℒA,\displaystyle=(\nabla_{f}\mathcal{L}^{B})^{T}\underbrace{\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}f^{B}(\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}f^{A})^{T}}_{=:\,\Theta^{AB}}\,\nabla_{f}\mathcal{L}^{A}\,, (18)

where we have defined the empirical NTK between batches AA and BB as ΘA​B=∇𝜽fB​(∇𝜽fA)T∈ℝm​|B|×m​|A|\Theta^{AB}=\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}f^{B}(\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}f^{A})^{T}\in\mathbb{R}^{m|B|\times m|A|}. It is important to note that for mini-batch training with A≠BA\neq B, the matrix ΘA​B\Theta^{AB} is not necessarily symmetric or positive semi-definite, in contrast to the full-batch empirical NTK with A=BA=B. To proceed, we perform an eigendecomposition onto the basis of ΘA​A\Theta^{AA} and ΘB​B\Theta^{BB}:

δ​ℒ​(A,B)\displaystyle\delta\mathcal{L}(A,B) =∑k,l(∇fTℒB​qkB)​[(qkB)T​ΘA​B​qlA]​(∇fTℒA​qlA)\displaystyle=\sum_{k,l}(\nabla_{f}^{T}\mathcal{L}^{B}\,q_{k}^{B})\,\left[(q_{k}^{B})^{T}\,\Theta^{AB}\,q_{l}^{A}\right]\,(\nabla_{f}^{T}\mathcal{L}^{A}\,q_{l}^{A}) (19)

where qkAq_{k}^{A} and qkBq_{k}^{B} are the eigenvectors of ΘA​A\Theta^{AA} and ΘB​B\Theta^{BB}, respectively.

LNP-decomposition for Full-Batch Training.

Equation 19 generalizes Equation 6 to mini-batch training. This can be seen by noting that for full-batch training with A=BA=B, the matrix ΘA​B\Theta^{AB} becomes symmetric and positive semi-definite Θ:=ΘA​A=ΘB​B\Theta:=\Theta^{AA}=\Theta^{BB}, allowing us to choose the same eigenbasis for both sides, i.e., qkA=qkB=qkq_{k}^{A}=q_{k}^{B}=q_{k}. The kernel then projects onto its eigenmodes qkT​Θ​ql=λk​δk​lq_{k}^{T}\,\Theta\,q_{l}=\lambda_{k}\,\delta_{kl}, yielding Equation 6:

δ​ℒ=∑k(∇fTℒ​qk)2​λk\delta\mathcal{L}=\sum_{k}(\nabla_{f}^{T}\mathcal{L}\,q_{k})^{2}\,\lambda_{k}\, (20)

In that case, the eigenvectors qkq_{k} form a complete orthonormal basis, and the projections of the loss gradient onto this basis satisfy

∑k(∇fTℒ​qk)2=‖∇fℒ‖22,\sum_{k}(\nabla_{f}^{T}\mathcal{L}\,q_{k})^{2}=\left\|\nabla_{f}\mathcal{L}\right\|_{2}^{2}\,, (21)

which is the squared magnitude of the loss gradient with respect to the network outputs and identifies the scale contribution of the loss function. Similarly, the eigenvalues λk\lambda_{k} satisfy

∑kλk=Tr​(Θ)=‖∇𝜽f‖F2\sum_{k}\lambda_{k}=\text{Tr}(\Theta)=\left\|\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}f\right\|_{F}^{2}\, (22)

where ‖∇𝜽f‖F2\left\|\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}f\right\|_{F}^{2} is the squared Frobenius norm of the Jacobian of the network outputs with respect to the parameters. This term captures the overall sensitivity of the network outputs to parameter changes, and identifies the scale contribution of the network. Using these relations, we can factorize both scale contributions from the sum in Equation 6 to obtain the LNP-decomposition:

δ​ℒ\displaystyle\delta\mathcal{L} =‖∇fℒ‖22⏟=:χloss‖∇θf‖F2⏟=:χnet∑k(∇fTℒ​qk)2‖∇fℒ‖22​λk‖∇θf‖F2⏟=:χpos=χloss⋅χnet⋅χpos,\displaystyle=\underbrace{\left\|\nabla_{f}\mathcal{L}\right\|_{2}^{2}}_{=:\,\chi_{\text{loss}}}\,\underbrace{\left\|\nabla_{\theta}f\right\|_{F}^{2}}_{=:\,\chi_{\text{net}}}\,\underbrace{\sum_{k}\frac{(\nabla_{f}^{T}\mathcal{L}\,q_{k})^{2}}{\left\|\nabla_{f}\mathcal{L}\right\|_{2}^{2}}\frac{\lambda_{k}}{\left\|\nabla_{\theta}f\right\|_{F}^{2}}}_{=:\,\chi_{\text{pos}}}=\,\chi_{\text{loss}}\cdot\chi_{\text{net}}\cdot\chi_{\text{pos}}\,, (23)

Factorizing out the two scale contributions yields a third component χpos\chi_{\text{pos}} that captures the interaction between the network and the loss function through the eNTK’s spectral properties. This component is scale-free and takes values in the range χpos∈[0,1]\chi_{\text{pos}}\in[0,1]. For more information on the interpretation of the LNP-components, we refer to Section 3.

LNP-decomposition for Mini-Batch Training.

For mini-batch training, the parameter update is carried out on batch AA and the loss change is evaluated on batch BB with A≠BA\neq B. We proceed similarly by factorizing the scale contributions from Equation 19:

δ​ℒ​(A,B)\displaystyle\delta\mathcal{L}(A,B) =‖∇fℒB‖2​‖∇fℒA‖2⏟=:χlossA​B‖∇θfB‖F​‖∇θfA‖F⏟=:χnetA​B∑k,l(∇fTℒB​qkB)‖∇fℒB‖2​(∇fTℒA​qlA)‖∇fℒA‖2​(qkB)T​ΘA​B​qlA‖∇θfB‖F​‖∇θfA‖F⏟=:χposA​B\displaystyle=\underbrace{\left\|\nabla_{f}\mathcal{L}^{B}\right\|_{2}\,\left\|\nabla_{f}\mathcal{L}^{A}\right\|_{2}}_{=:\,\chi_{\text{loss}}^{AB}}\,\underbrace{\left\|\nabla_{\theta}f^{B}\right\|_{F}\,\left\|\nabla_{\theta}f^{A}\right\|_{F}}_{=:\,\chi_{\text{net}}^{AB}}\,\underbrace{\sum_{k,l}\frac{(\nabla_{f}^{T}\mathcal{L}^{B}\,q_{k}^{B})}{\left\|\nabla_{f}\mathcal{L}^{B}\right\|_{2}}\,\frac{(\nabla_{f}^{T}\mathcal{L}^{A}\,q_{l}^{A})}{\left\|\nabla_{f}\mathcal{L}^{A}\right\|_{2}}\,\frac{(q_{k}^{B})^{T}\,\Theta^{AB}\,q_{l}^{A}}{\left\|\nabla_{\theta}f^{B}\right\|_{F}\,\left\|\nabla_{\theta}f^{A}\right\|_{F}}}_{=:\,\chi_{\text{pos}}^{AB}}
=χlossA​B⋅χnetA​B⋅χposA​B.\displaystyle=\,\chi_{\text{loss}}^{AB}\cdot\chi_{\text{net}}^{AB}\cdot\chi_{\text{pos}}^{AB}\,. (24)

This expression generalizes the LNP-decomposition to mini-batch training, where each component now depends on both batches AA and BB. We obtain a contribution of loss and network magnitude from both batches and a spectral position component χposA​B\chi_{\text{pos}}^{AB} that captures the interaction between the two batches through the mixed eNTK ΘA​B\Theta^{AB}. Note that the projections of the loss onto the eigenbases ∇fTℒB​qkB\nabla_{f}^{T}\mathcal{L}^{B}\,q_{k}^{B} and ∇fTℒA​qlA\nabla_{f}^{T}\mathcal{L}^{A}\,q_{l}^{A} can now result in negative values. Similarly, the mixed eNTK projections (qkB)T​ΘA​B​qlA(q_{k}^{B})^{T}\,\Theta^{AB}\,q_{l}^{A} can also be negative. If the spectral position contribution χposA​Bk​l{\chi_{\text{pos}}^{AB}}_{kl} of a specific mode pair (k,l)(k,l) satisfies

χposA​Bk​l=(∇fTℒB​qkB)‖∇fℒB‖2​(∇fTℒA​qlA)‖∇fℒA‖2​(qkB)T​ΘA​B​qlA‖∇θfB‖F​‖∇θfA‖F<0,{\chi_{\text{pos}}^{AB}}_{kl}=\frac{(\nabla_{f}^{T}\mathcal{L}^{B}\,q_{k}^{B})}{\left\|\nabla_{f}\mathcal{L}^{B}\right\|_{2}}\,\frac{(\nabla_{f}^{T}\mathcal{L}^{A}\,q_{l}^{A})}{\left\|\nabla_{f}\mathcal{L}^{A}\right\|_{2}}\,\frac{(q_{k}^{B})^{T}\,\Theta^{AB}\,q_{l}^{A}}{\left\|\nabla_{\theta}f^{B}\right\|_{F}\,\left\|\nabla_{\theta}f^{A}\right\|_{F}}<0\,, (25)

it means that the mode ll resulting from training on AA has a detrimental effect on the mode kk in BB. This happens when information learned from batch AA does not generalize to batch BB or even interferes destructively, which occurs e.g. in unlearning and overfitting scenarios.

As this work is focused on pre-training settings with large and diverse datasets, we expect most mode pairs to contribute positively to the spectral position, i.e., χposA​Bk​l>0{\chi_{\text{pos}}^{AB}}_{kl}>0. Comparing Figures 1 and 7, we see that train and test losses yield the same quantitative scaling ratios. This means that training seems to converge before overfitting effects occur, which supports our assumption of positive spectral position contributions.

A.2 Normalization of LNP-Components

In this section, we provide further details how to normalize the LNP-components introduced in Section 3 and Appendix A.1 to remove batch-size dependencies.

The LNP-decomposition factors the linearized loss change into three components

δ​ℒ​(A,B)=χlossA​B⋅χnetA​B⋅χposA​B.\delta\mathcal{L}(A,B)=\chi_{\text{loss}}^{AB}\cdot\chi_{\text{net}}^{AB}\cdot\chi_{\text{pos}}^{AB}\,. (26)

However, with the definition provided in Equation 24, the loss and network magnitudes χlossA​B\chi_{\text{loss}}^{AB} and χnetA​B\chi_{\text{net}}^{AB} depend on the batch sizes |A||A| and |B||B|. This can be understood by rewriting into sample-wise contributions. For a loss function of the form ℒB=1|B|​∑i∈Bℒ⁡(f⁡(𝐱i),yi)\mathcal{L}^{B}=\frac{1}{|B|}\sum_{i\in B}\mathcal{L}(f(\mathbf{x}_{i}),y_{i}), we can express the loss magnitude component ‖∇fℒB‖2\left\|\nabla_{f}\mathcal{L}^{B}\right\|_{2} as sample-wise sum

‖∇fℒB‖2=1|B|2​∑i∈B‖∇f⁡(𝐱i)ℒ‖22=1|B|​1|B|​∑i∈B‖∇f⁡(𝐱i)ℒ‖22=1|B|​σlossB,\left\|\nabla_{f}\mathcal{L}^{B}\right\|_{2}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{|B|^{2}}\sum_{i\in B}\left\|\nabla_{f(\mathbf{x}_{i})}\mathcal{L}\right\|_{2}^{2}}\,=\frac{1}{\sqrt{|B|}}\,\sqrt{\frac{1}{|B|}\sum_{i\in B}\left\|\nabla_{f(\mathbf{x}_{i})}\mathcal{L}\right\|_{2}^{2}}\,=\frac{1}{\sqrt{|B|}}\,\sigma_{\text{loss}}^{B}\,, (27)

where σlossB\sigma_{\text{loss}}^{B} is the standard deviation of the sample-wise loss gradients in batch BB. In expectation of large batch sizes, this quantity converges to the population standard deviation of the loss gradients over the data distribution. Thus, the loss magnitude scales with the inverse square root of the batch size ‖∇fℒB‖2∝1|B|\left\|\nabla_{f}\mathcal{L}^{B}\right\|_{2}\propto\frac{1}{\sqrt{|B|}}.

Looking at the network magnitude ‖∇θfB‖F\left\|\nabla_{\theta}f^{B}\right\|_{F}, we can perform a similar derivation:

‖∇θfB‖F=∑i∈B‖∇θf​(𝐱i)‖22=|B|​1|B|​∑i∈B‖∇θf​(𝐱i)‖22=|B|​σnetB,\left\|\nabla_{\theta}f^{B}\right\|_{F}=\sqrt{\sum_{i\in B}\left\|\nabla_{\theta}f(\mathbf{x}_{i})\right\|_{2}^{2}}\,=\sqrt{|B|}\,\sqrt{\frac{1}{|B|}\sum_{i\in B}\left\|\nabla_{\theta}f(\mathbf{x}_{i})\right\|_{2}^{2}}\,=\sqrt{|B|}\,\sigma_{\text{net}}^{B}\,, (28)

where σnetB\sigma_{\text{net}}^{B} is the standard deviation of the sample-wise network gradients in batch BB. In expectation of large batch sizes, this quantity converges to the population standard deviation of the network gradients over the data distribution. Thus, the network magnitude scales with the square root of the batch size ‖∇θfB‖F∝|B|\left\|\nabla_{\theta}f^{B}\right\|_{F}\propto\sqrt{|B|}.

To remove these batch-size dependencies, we can move the batch-size scaling factors from the loss into the network magnitude, yielding normalized LNP-components:

δ​ℒ​(A,B)\displaystyle\delta\mathcal{L}(A,B) =|A|​|B|​χlossA​B⏟=:χ~lossA​BχnetA​B|A|​|B|⏟=:χ~netA​BχposA​B\displaystyle=\underbrace{\sqrt{|A|\,|B|}\,\chi_{\text{loss}}^{AB}}_{=:\,\tilde{\chi}_{\text{loss}}^{AB}}\,\underbrace{\frac{\chi_{\text{net}}^{AB}}{\sqrt{|A|\,|B|}}}_{=:\,\tilde{\chi}_{\text{net}}^{AB}}\,\chi_{\text{pos}}^{AB}\, (29)

In practice, we use these normalized LNP-components χ~lossA​B\tilde{\chi}_{\text{loss}}^{AB} and χ~netA​B\tilde{\chi}_{\text{net}}^{AB} to analyze training dynamics across different batch sizes.

A.3 Connection to Kernel-Target Alignment

χpos\chi_{\text{pos}} indicates which eigenvalues of the eNTK currently drive loss reduction (Section 3). Since this involves the eNTK and the loss-gradient direction together, a natural question is how it relates to kernel-alignment metrics. The kernel-target alignment of Cristianini et al. (2001) and its follow-ups (Cortes et al., 2012; Baratin et al., 2021) provide a general framework for the affinity between two positive semi-definite matrices, typically a kernel and a task-defined target. χpos\chi_{\text{pos}} corresponds to a specific instance of this idea (loss gradient as target, eNTK as kernel) with a different normalization, which arises naturally from the LNP-decomposition. Below we make the connection explicit.

χpos\chi_{\text{pos}} as a Matrix-Alignment Ratio.

With slight abuse of notation, AA and BB in this subsection denote the two matrices being compared, not the batch indices used in Appendices A.1 and A.2. Define

A\displaystyle A =∇fℒ​(∇fℒ)T∈ℝn​m×n​m,\displaystyle=\nabla_{f}\mathcal{L}\,(\nabla_{f}\mathcal{L})^{T}\in\mathbb{R}^{nm\times nm}, (30)
B\displaystyle B =Θ∈ℝn​m×n​m,\displaystyle=\Theta\in\mathbb{R}^{nm\times nm}, (31)

where nn is the batch size and mm the per-sample output dimension. Both AA and BB are positive semi-definite, and AA is rank-1 by construction: it is the outer product of g=∇fℒ∈ℝn​mg=\nabla_{f}\mathcal{L}\in\mathbb{R}^{nm} with itself.

Recall from Section 3 that δ​ℒ=(∇fℒ)T​Θ​∇fℒ=Tr​(A​B)\delta\mathcal{L}=(\nabla_{f}\mathcal{L})^{T}\Theta\,\nabla_{f}\mathcal{L}=\text{Tr}(AB), χloss=‖∇fℒ‖22=Tr​(A)\chi_{\text{loss}}=\|\nabla_{f}\mathcal{L}\|_{2}^{2}=\text{Tr}(A), and χnet=‖∇θf‖F2=Tr​(Θ)=Tr​(B)\chi_{\text{net}}=\|\nabla_{\theta}f\|_{F}^{2}=\text{Tr}(\Theta)=\text{Tr}(B). Substituting these identities into the LNP-decomposition,

χpos=δ​ℒχloss⋅χnet=Tr​(A​B)Tr​(A)⋅Tr​(B).\chi_{\text{pos}}=\frac{\delta\mathcal{L}}{\chi_{\text{loss}}\cdot\chi_{\text{net}}}=\frac{\text{Tr}(AB)}{\text{Tr}(A)\cdot\text{Tr}(B)}. (32)

χpos\chi_{\text{pos}} is therefore a ratio between the matrix overlap Tr​(A​B)\text{Tr}(AB) and the product of the two traces.

Relation to Cristianini’s Kernel-Target Alignment.

Cristianini’s measure normalizes by Frobenius norms instead of traces:

Sim​(A,B)=Tr​(A​B)‖A‖F​‖B‖F=Tr​(A​B)Tr​(A2)⋅Tr​(B2).\text{Sim}(A,B)=\frac{\text{Tr}(AB)}{\|A\|_{F}\,\|B\|_{F}}=\frac{\text{Tr}(AB)}{\sqrt{\text{Tr}(A^{2})}\cdot\sqrt{\text{Tr}(B^{2})}}. (33)

The two measures share the numerator Tr​(A​B)\text{Tr}(AB) and differ only in their denominators. The loss-side denominator simplifies because AA is rank-1: with A=g​gTA=gg^{T}, the matrix product reduces to A2=g⁡(gT​g)​gT=‖g‖2​AA^{2}=g(g^{T}g)g^{T}=\|g\|^{2}A. Taking the trace,

Tr​(A2)=‖g‖2​Tr​(A)=‖g‖4=Tr​(A)2,\text{Tr}(A^{2})=\|g\|^{2}\,\text{Tr}(A)=\|g\|^{4}=\text{Tr}(A)^{2}, (34)

so Tr​(A2)=Tr​(A)\sqrt{\text{Tr}(A^{2})}=\text{Tr}(A). The two denominators therefore agree on the loss side; the only difference lies in how Θ\Theta is normalized: χpos\chi_{\text{pos}} uses Tr​(Θ)\text{Tr}(\Theta), while Sim​(A,B)\text{Sim}(A,B) uses ‖Θ‖F=Tr​(Θ2)\|\Theta\|_{F}=\sqrt{\text{Tr}(\Theta^{2})}. The exact relationship is

χpos=Sim​(A,B)⋅‖Θ‖FTr​(Θ).\chi_{\text{pos}}=\text{Sim}(A,B)\cdot\frac{\|\Theta\|_{F}}{\text{Tr}(\Theta)}. (35)
Spectral Interpretation of the Extra Factor.

Writing Θ=∑kλk​qk​qkT\Theta=\sum_{k}\lambda_{k}\,q_{k}q_{k}^{T} with eigenvalues λk≥0\lambda_{k}\geq 0, we have Tr​(Θ)=∑kλk\text{Tr}(\Theta)=\sum_{k}\lambda_{k} and ‖Θ‖F2=∑kλk2\|\Theta\|_{F}^{2}=\sum_{k}\lambda_{k}^{2}. By the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality (∑kλk)2≤n​m​∑kλk2(\sum_{k}\lambda_{k})^{2}\leq nm\,\sum_{k}\lambda_{k}^{2}, so

‖Θ‖FTr​(Θ)∈[1n​m, 1],\frac{\|\Theta\|_{F}}{\text{Tr}(\Theta)}\in\left[\frac{1}{\sqrt{nm}},\,1\right], (36)

with the lower bound attained when all eigenvalues are equal (maximally spread spectrum) and the upper bound when one eigenvalue dominates (maximally concentrated spectrum). Equivalently, with normalized eigenvalues pk=λk/Tr​(Θ)p_{k}=\lambda_{k}/\text{Tr}(\Theta), the eNTK’s inverse participation ratio is IPR​(Θ)=∑kpk2=‖Θ‖F2/Tr​(Θ)2\text{IPR}(\Theta)=\sum_{k}p_{k}^{2}=\|\Theta\|_{F}^{2}/\text{Tr}(\Theta)^{2}, so

‖Θ‖FTr​(Θ)=IPR​(Θ).\frac{\|\Theta\|_{F}}{\text{Tr}(\Theta)}=\sqrt{\text{IPR}(\Theta)}. (37)

The factor measures spectral concentration of the eNTK: small when eigenvalues are spread out, large when they cluster on a small effective subspace.

Spectral position therefore jointly captures the directional alignment between the loss gradient and the eNTK eigenmodes and the spectral concentration of the eNTK itself. The trace-based normalization is not arbitrary: it arises from the LNP factorization derived in Section 3 and is what guarantees the bounded range χpos∈[0,1]\chi_{\text{pos}}\in[0,1].

A.4 Derivation of Spectral Scaling Relationships for RFMs

This section derives the theoretical scaling relationship between the data spectral exponent β\beta and the loss-network-position (LNP) decomposition components. We analyze a teacher-student setting for random feature models (RFMs) in the infinite-width limit.

Notation note.

This subsection and the corresponding experimental details in Appendix B.2.5 adopt standard random-feature / kernel-methods conventions: nn denotes the dataset size, mm the width, 𝐰j\mathbf{w}_{j} a frozen random feature, and 𝐜\mathbf{c} the trainable readout weights. These differ from the NTK notation in Appendices A.1–A.3.

A.4.1 Setup and Definitions

We consider a dataset 𝒟={(𝐱i,yi)}i=1n\mathcal{D}=\{(\mathbf{x}_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n} where inputs 𝐱∈ℝd\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} are drawn i.i.d. from a centered Gaussian distribution 𝒩⁡(0,𝚺)\mathcal{N}(0,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}) with trace normalized to dd. The model is a random feature model in the infinite-width limit (m→∞m\to\infty), which is equivalent to a kernel regression method with the limiting kernel:

K⁡(𝐱,𝐱′)=𝔼𝐰∼𝒩⁡(0,d−1​𝐈)​[σ⁡(𝐰⊤​𝐱)​σ​(𝐰⊤​𝐱′)],K(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{w}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,d^{-1}\mathbf{I})}\left[\sigma(\mathbf{w}^{\top}\mathbf{x})\sigma(\mathbf{w}^{\top}\mathbf{x}^{\prime})\right], (38)

where σ⁡(⋅)\sigma(\cdot) is the variance-preserving ReLU activation σ⁡(z)=2​max⁡(0,z)\sigma(z)=\sqrt{2}\max(0,z). We denote the kernel Gram matrix as 𝐊∈ℝn×n\mathbf{K}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} with entries Ki​j=K⁡(𝐱i,𝐱j)K_{ij}=K(\mathbf{x}_{i},\mathbf{x}_{j}). The network is trained to minimize the Mean Squared Error (MSE):

ℒ⁡(𝐜)=12​n​‖𝐲−f⁡(𝐗,𝐜)‖2.\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{c})=\frac{1}{2n}\|\mathbf{y}-f(\mathbf{X};\mathbf{c})\|^{2}. (39)

A.4.2 Loss Dynamics at Initialization

We analyze the change in loss Δ​ℒ\Delta\mathcal{L} after a single gradient descent step with learning rate η\eta, starting from zero initialization (𝐜0=𝟎\mathbf{c}_{0}=\mathbf{0}). The network output after one step is f1​(𝐗)=ηn​𝐊𝐲f_{1}(\mathbf{X})=\frac{\eta}{n}\mathbf{K}\mathbf{y}. The exact change in loss is:

Δ​ℒ\displaystyle\Delta\mathcal{L} =ℒ⁡(𝐜1)−ℒ⁡(𝟎)\displaystyle=\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{c}_{1})-\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{0})
=12​n​‖𝐲−ηn​𝐊𝐲‖2−12​n​‖𝐲‖2\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2n}\left\|\mathbf{y}-\frac{\eta}{n}\mathbf{K}\mathbf{y}\right\|^{2}-\frac{1}{2n}\|\mathbf{y}\|^{2}
=−ηn2​𝐲⊤​𝐊𝐲+η22​n3​𝐲⊤​𝐊2​𝐲.\displaystyle=-\frac{\eta}{n^{2}}\mathbf{y}^{\top}\mathbf{K}\mathbf{y}+\frac{\eta^{2}}{2n^{3}}\mathbf{y}^{\top}\mathbf{K}^{2}\mathbf{y}. (40)

In the small learning rate regime, the linear term dominates. We focus on the normalized initial slope of the loss:

−Δ​ℒη≈1n2​𝐲⊤​𝐊𝐲.-\frac{\Delta\mathcal{L}}{\eta}\approx\frac{1}{n^{2}}\mathbf{y}^{\top}\mathbf{K}\mathbf{y}. (41)

A.4.3 LNP-Decomposition

We decompose the driving term 1n2​𝐲⊤​𝐊𝐲\frac{1}{n^{2}}\mathbf{y}^{\top}\mathbf{K}\mathbf{y} into the three scalar components: loss magnitude χloss\chi_{\text{loss}}, network magnitude χnet\chi_{\text{net}}, and spectral position χpos\chi_{\text{pos}}. Using the eigendecomposition 𝐊=∑kλ^k​𝐯k​𝐯k⊤\mathbf{K}=\sum_{k}\hat{\lambda}_{k}\mathbf{v}_{k}\mathbf{v}_{k}^{\top} and projecting the targets onto the eigenbasis as αk=𝐯k⊤​𝐲\alpha_{k}=\mathbf{v}_{k}^{\top}\mathbf{y}, we factorize as follows:

𝐲⊤​𝐊𝐲n2=(‖𝐲‖2n)⏟χloss⋅(Tr​(𝐊)n)⏟χnet⋅(∑k=1nαk2‖𝐲‖2​λ^kTr​(𝐊))⏟χpos.\frac{\mathbf{y}^{\top}\mathbf{K}\mathbf{y}}{n^{2}}=\underbrace{\left(\frac{\|\mathbf{y}\|^{2}}{n}\right)}_{\chi_{\text{loss}}}\cdot\underbrace{\left(\frac{\text{Tr}(\mathbf{K})}{n}\right)}_{\chi_{\text{net}}}\cdot\underbrace{\left(\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{\alpha_{k}^{2}}{\|\mathbf{y}\|^{2}}\frac{\hat{\lambda}_{k}}{\text{Tr}(\mathbf{K})}\right)}_{\chi_{\text{pos}}}. (42)

A.4.4 Component Analysis in the Large Sample Limit

We evaluate the expectation of each component over the data and teacher distributions in the large nn limit.

1. Loss Component (χloss\chi_{\text{loss}}).

We construct targets to be standardized such that var​(y)=1\text{var}(y)=1. Implementation details can be found in Section B.2.5. Consequently, by the Law of Large Numbers:

χloss=1n​∑i=1nyi2→n→∞𝔼⁡[y2]=1.\chi_{\text{loss}}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}y_{i}^{2}\xrightarrow{n\to\infty}\mathbb{E}[y^{2}]=1. (43)
2. Network Component (χnet\chi_{\text{net}}).

The trace term averages the kernel diagonal: χnet=1n​∑iK⁡(𝐱i,𝐱i)\chi_{\text{net}}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}K(\mathbf{x}_{i},\mathbf{x}_{i}). For ReLU features with normalized weights 𝐰∼𝒩⁡(0,d−1​𝐈)\mathbf{w}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,d^{-1}\mathbf{I}) and data covariance Tr​(𝚺)=d\text{Tr}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma})=d:

𝔼⁡[χnet]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\chi_{\text{net}}] =𝔼𝐱,𝐰​[σ​(𝐰⊤​𝐱)2]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{w}}[\sigma(\mathbf{w}^{\top}\mathbf{x})^{2}]
=12𝔼[(𝐰⊤𝐱)2]⋅2(symmetry of distribution around 0)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}[(\mathbf{w}^{\top}\mathbf{x})^{2}]\cdot 2\quad\text{(symmetry of distribution around 0)}
=Tr​(𝔼⁡[𝐱𝐱⊤]​𝔼​[𝐰𝐰⊤])=Tr​(𝚺⋅1d​𝐈)=1.\displaystyle=\text{Tr}\left(\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}\mathbf{x}^{\top}]\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{w}\mathbf{w}^{\top}]\right)=\text{Tr}\left(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\cdot\frac{1}{d}\mathbf{I}\right)=1. (44)

Thus, χnet→1\chi_{\text{net}}\to 1.

3. Spectral Position Component (χpos\chi_{\text{pos}}).

This component captures how the target energy is distributed across the kernel’s eigenmodes. We adopt a Gaussian Process Teacher setting, where f∗∼𝒢​𝒫​(0,K)f^{*}\sim\mathcal{GP}(0,K). This implies that the vector of targets on the training set follows 𝐲∼𝒩⁡(0,𝐊)\mathbf{y}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{K}). In the eigenbasis of 𝐊\mathbf{K}, the projection coefficients αk\alpha_{k} are independent Gaussian variables with variance equal to the eigenvalues:

𝔼⁡[αk2]=λ^k.\mathbb{E}[\alpha_{k}^{2}]=\hat{\lambda}_{k}. (45)

Substituting this into the definition of χpos\chi_{\text{pos}} and invoking the concentration of spectral sums for large nn (replacing empirical λ^\hat{\lambda} with population λ\lambda):

𝔼⁡[χpos]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\chi_{\text{pos}}] =𝔼⁡[∑kαk2​λ^k‖𝐲‖2​Tr​(𝐊)]≈∑k𝔼⁡[αk2]​λk𝔼⁡[‖𝐲‖2]​∑jλj\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\sum_{k}\alpha_{k}^{2}\hat{\lambda}_{k}}{\|\mathbf{y}\|^{2}\text{Tr}(\mathbf{K})}\right]\approx\frac{\sum_{k}\mathbb{E}[\alpha_{k}^{2}]\lambda_{k}}{\mathbb{E}[\|\mathbf{y}\|^{2}]\sum_{j}\lambda_{j}}
∝∑kλk2(∑kλk)2.\displaystyle\propto\frac{\sum_{k}\lambda_{k}^{2}}{(\sum_{k}\lambda_{k})^{2}}. (46)

This result identifies χpos\chi_{\text{pos}} as the inverse effective dimension (or participation ratio) of the kernel spectrum.

A.4.5 Spectral Transfer and Final Scaling

Finally, we relate the kernel eigenvalues λk\lambda_{k} to the data covariance spectrum μk\mu_{k}. We assume the data spectrum follows a power law μk∼k−β\mu_{k}\sim k^{-\beta} with β>1\beta>1.

Linear Dominance Principle.

The kernel KK admits a Mercer decomposition based on the Hermite expansion of the ReLU activation. The nn-th order term in the expansion depends on the nn-th tensor power of the data covariance. Crucially, for ReLU, the first Hermite coefficient is non-zero (h1≠0h_{1}\neq 0). Higher-order terms (n≥2n\geq 2) correspond to symmetric tensor powers of 𝚺\boldsymbol{\Sigma}. For a data spectrum μk∝k−β\mu_{k}\propto k^{-\beta} with β>1\beta>1, the sorted eigenvalues of the nn-th tensor power decay asymptotically faster than the linear term (Canatar et al., 2021; Scetbon and Harchaoui, 2021). Specifically, the spectral density of the product of power-law variables yields a tail behavior dominated by the linear component, establishing the linear dominance principle. Therefore, the kernel spectrum inherits the asymptotic decay rate of the data:

λk∼μk∼k−β.\lambda_{k}\sim\mu_{k}\sim k^{-\beta}. (47)
Final Scaling Law.

Substituting λk∝k−β\lambda_{k}\propto k^{-\beta} into the expression for spectral position:

χpos∝∑k=1∞k−2​β(∑k=1∞k−β)2.\chi_{\text{pos}}\propto\frac{\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}k^{-2\beta}}{\left(\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}k^{-\beta}\right)^{2}}. (48)

This concludes the derivation, explicitly linking the initial optimization dynamics to the spectral exponent β\beta via χpos\chi_{\text{pos}}.

Appendix B Experimental Details

B.1 Computation of LNP-Components

In this section, we provide further details on the computational aspects of measuring the LNP-components introduced in Section 3 and Appendix A.1.

Efficient Computation without Explicit eNTK Formation.

We will now discuss how to compute the LNP-components efficiently without explicitly forming the empirical Neural Tangent Kernel (eNTK) matrix, which can be computationally prohibitive for large models. The spectral position component χposA​B\chi_{\text{pos}}^{AB} in the LNP-decomposition in Equation 24 naively requires the full eNTK computation, which would be prohibitively expensive for large-scale models. However, we can compute it indirectly by rearranging the LNP-decomposition:

χposA​B=δ​ℒ​(A,B)χlossA​B⋅χnetA​B.\chi_{\text{pos}}^{AB}=\frac{\delta\mathcal{L}(A,B)}{\chi_{\text{loss}}^{AB}\cdot\chi_{\text{net}}^{AB}}\,. (49)

This rearrangement allows us to efficiently obtain χposA​B\chi_{\text{pos}}^{AB} by computing the three quantities on the right-hand side separately.

We now describe how each of these components is measured in practice. The linearized loss change δ​ℒ​(A,B)\delta\mathcal{L}(A,B) is simply computed as the inner product of two parameter gradients

δ​ℒ​(A,B)=∇𝜽TℒB​∇𝜽ℒA,\delta\mathcal{L}(A,B)=\nabla^{T}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}^{B}\,\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}^{A}\,, (50)

which can be efficiently computed using standard backpropagation.

For the loss and network magnitudes χlossA​B\chi_{\text{loss}}^{AB} and χnetA​B\chi_{\text{net}}^{AB}, we refer to their definition in Equation 24. Computing each of these components requires evaluating two terms: one on batch AA and one on batch BB. For instance, the loss magnitude is given by χlossA​B=‖∇fℒB‖2​‖∇fℒA‖2\chi_{\text{loss}}^{AB}=\left\|\nabla_{f}\mathcal{L}^{B}\right\|_{2}\,\left\|\nabla_{f}\mathcal{L}^{A}\right\|_{2}, requiring the computation of the loss gradient norm on both batches. Similarly, the network magnitude χnetA​B=‖∇θfB‖F​‖∇θfA‖F\chi_{\text{net}}^{AB}=\left\|\nabla_{\theta}f^{B}\right\|_{F}\,\left\|\nabla_{\theta}f^{A}\right\|_{F} requires computing the Frobenius norm of the network Jacobian on both batches.

As shown in Equations 27 and 28, these magnitudes can be rewritten in terms of sample-wise gradient norms. In the field of differential privacy, efficient techniques have been developed to compute sample-wise gradient norms without explicitly forming the full Jacobian matrices ∇θfA\nabla_{\theta}f^{A} and ∇θfB\nabla_{\theta}f^{B} (Abadi et al., 2016; Goodfellow, 2015; Rochette et al., 2019; Lee and Kifer, 2020). Efficient implementations are available in popular deep learning frameworks such as Opacus (Yousefpour et al., 2022).

With this framework at hand, we can compute all three LNP-components efficiently without explicitly forming the eNTK matrix, enabling their application to large-scale models where eNTK computations become impractical.

Hutchinson’s Trace Estimation with Opacus (Yousefpour et al., 2022).

We implement the per-sample computation of the LNP-components using the Opacus library. While this allows for very efficient sample-wise gradient norms of one-dimensional functions, a naive implementation would require separate backward passes for each output dimension to calculate the sample-wise gradients ∇𝜽f​(𝐱i)\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}f(\mathbf{x}_{i}) when the network outputs are multi-dimensional. This can significantly increase the computational cost when the output dimension mm is large, as e.g. in language modeling where it is equal to the vocabulary size i.e. m>104m>10^{4}. To avoid computing separate backward passes for each output dimension, we apply Hutchinson’s trace estimator (Hutchinson, 1990) to estimate the squared norm of the sample-wise gradients with respect to multi-dimensional outputs. Mathematically, we estimate the squared norm of the sample-wise gradients as

‖∇𝜽fA​(𝐱i)‖F2=Tr​(∇𝜽fA​(𝐱i)​∇𝜽TfA​(𝐱i))≈1M​∑m=1MvmT​∇𝜽fA​(𝐱i)​∇𝜽TfA​(𝐱i)​vm=1M​∑m=1M(vmT​∇𝜽fA​(𝐱i))2,\left\|\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}f^{A}(\mathbf{x}_{i})\right\|_{F}^{2}=\text{Tr}\left(\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}f^{A}(\mathbf{x}_{i})\,\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{T}f^{A}(\mathbf{x}_{i})\right)\approx\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M}v_{m}^{T}\,\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}f^{A}(\mathbf{x}_{i})\,\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{T}f^{A}(\mathbf{x}_{i})\,v_{m}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M}\left(v_{m}^{T}\,\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}f^{A}(\mathbf{x}_{i})\right)^{2}\,, (51)

where vm∈ℝmv_{m}\in\mathbb{R}^{m} are random Rademacher vectors (entries sampled from {−1,1}\{-1,1\} with equal probability) and MM is the number of random vectors used for the estimation. This approach allows us to estimate the squared norm of the sample-wise gradients with only MM backward passes per batch, significantly reducing the computational overhead compared to computing exact sample-wise gradients for multi-dimensional outputs.

Convergence of the Hutchinson Estimator.

We choose M=10M=10 Rademacher projections as a practical trade-off between accuracy and per-step cost; Figure 6 validates this choice. The single-step coefficient of variation of the estimated squared gradient norm is approximately 23%23\% at M=10M=10 (top right). Because the LNP-components reported in this work are averaged over windows of 5050 training steps with independent Rademacher draws at each step, the effective coefficient of variation reduces to 23%/50≈3.3%23\%/\sqrt{50}\approx 3.3\%, comparable to the 3.1%3.1\% obtained at M=500M=500 projections per step but at 50×50\times lower per-step cost. The fitted 1/M1/\sqrt{M} decay (top right) matches the theoretical Hutchinson rate. The convergence study was conducted on a trained 7.27.2M-parameter model using 3232 training samples. The bottom panels confirm the practical consequence: χpos\chi_{\text{pos}} agrees tightly across 33 independent training seeds for all model sizes on both SimpleStories and CIFAR-5M.

Estimated Computational Overhead.

Using the techniques described above, we can compute the LNP-components with minimal computational overhead during training. In this section, we will show how to estimate the additional computational cost incurred by computing the LNP-components alongside standard training. First, we note that the LNP-components are not required to be computed at every training step. Instead, we compute them across windows of WW subsequent training steps. We choose these windows to be located at logarithmically spaced intervals during training, as the dynamics of training typically evolve more slowly at later stages. While we provide measurement details in Appendix B.2, we will use a typical setting to illustrate the computational overhead. We choose W=50W=50 training steps per window and S=20S=20 windows across training, resulting in a total of S⋅W=1000S\cdot W=1000 training steps with LNP measurements.

Next, we analyze the computational cost of computing the LNP-components at each training step within a window. The main additional cost arises from computing the sample-wise gradient norms using Hutchinson’s trace estimator with MM random vectors. This requires MM forward and backward passes per batch, and as explained in Appendix B.1, we need to compute these norms for both batches AA and BB, resulting in a total of 2​M2M forward and backward passes for computing the loss and network magnitudes. Additionally, we need to compute the inner product of the two parameter gradients to obtain δ​ℒ​(A,B)\delta\mathcal{L}(A,B), which requires two additional forward and backward passes. Overall, this results in a total of 2+2​M2+2M forward and backward passes per training step with LNP measurements.

Assume that we train for a total of T=100000T=100000 requiring the same number of forward and backward passes. If we choose M=10M=10 random vectors for the Hutchinson estimator, the total number of additional forward and backward passes for computing the LNP-components across all windows is

S⋅W⋅(2+2​M)=20⋅50⋅(2+20)=22000.S\cdot W\cdot(2+2M)=20\cdot 50\cdot(2+20)=22000\,. (52)

Thus, the total number of forward and backward passes during training with LNP measurements rises from 100,000100,000 to 122,000122,000, resulting in an estimated computational overhead of only 22%22\%.

Memory Overhead.

Storing sample-wise gradients for large models is efficiently handled by Opacus using gradient checkpointing and memory-efficient backpropagation techniques (Yousefpour et al., 2022). In the current implementation, the main memory overhead arises from storing a second parameter gradient in memory. This occurs when computing the inner product of the two parameter gradients to obtain δ​ℒ​(A,B)=∇𝜽TℒB​∇𝜽ℒA\delta\mathcal{L}(A,B)=\nabla^{T}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}^{B}\,\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}^{A}. Consequently, we obtain a memory increase of approximately 1×1\times the model size.

Comparison to Direct eNTK Methods.

The computational savings of the LNP-decomposition come from its structure, not from Hutchinson estimation alone. As shown in Section 3, χpos\chi_{\text{pos}} can be written as the scalar ratio δ​ℒ/(χloss⋅χnet)\delta\mathcal{L}/(\chi_{\text{loss}}\cdot\chi_{\text{net}}), where δ​ℒ=‖∇𝜽ℒ‖2\delta\mathcal{L}=\|\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}\|^{2} is a single scalar and χloss,χnet\chi_{\text{loss}},\chi_{\text{net}} reduce to sums of squared per-sample gradient norms. The cross-sample structure of the eNTK enters only implicitly through δ​ℒ\delta\mathcal{L}; no per-sample Jacobian and no kernel entry is ever materialized.

Methods that probe the eNTK directly do not admit this reduction. For example, kernel-target alignment (Cristianini et al., 2001; Baratin et al., 2021) requires the cross-sample entries of Θ\Theta explicitly, which in turn requires constructing per-sample Jacobians J∈ℝn​m×NJ\in\mathbb{R}^{nm\times N} at O⁡(n​m)O(nm) backward passes per batch, where nn is the batch size, mm the per-sample output dimension (vocab size ×\times sequence length for language models), and NN the number of model parameters. For LLMs with large vocab and long context, n​mnm reaches 10810^{8} or beyond, making direct eNTK computation prohibitive in both compute and memory.

By contrast, our per-step cost is O⁡(M)O(M) forward-backward passes (with M=10M=10 in our experiments), independent of n​mnm. For typical LLM settings, this amounts to a difference of several orders of magnitude per measured step.

B.2 Setups

In this section, we provide further details on the experimental setups used in our study. We choose the SimpleStories (Finke et al., 2025) and CIFAR-5M (Nakkiran et al., 2020) datasets because their modest computational requirements allow extensive experiments across multiple model sizes and training runs.

B.2.1 SimpleStories

The SimpleStories dataset is a collection of 2 million short stories with a custom tokenizer that reduces the vocabulary size to 4096 tokens (Finke et al., 2025). We train Llama 2 transformer models of varying sizes (1.2M, 2.1M, 3.8M, 7.2M, 15.5M, 31.5M, 65.6M, 134M parameters) on the next-token prediction task (Touvron et al., 2023). Model details are provided in Table 1.

We train each model for a single epoch using AdamW with weight decay 0.01, β1=0.9\beta_{1}=0.9, and β2=0.95\beta_{2}=0.95. We use learning rates (1e-2, 5e-3, 5e-3, 4e-3, 2e-3, 6e-4, 3e-4, 1.5e-4) for the different model sizes (in order of increasing size), selected via preliminary grid searches. We apply a linear learning-rate warmup over the first 100 steps. We use batch size 32, context length 512 tokens, and train for a total of 66116 steps. Experiments are repeated for 3 random model initializations, preserving the data order across runs.

We measure the LNP-components across logarithmically spaced windows during training. Specifically, we use S=24S=24 windows, each spanning W=50W=50 training steps. Because we compute the LNP-components only once within overlapping windows, this results in a total of 801801 training steps with LNP measurements. We use M=10M=10 random vectors for the Hutchinson estimator to compute sample-wise gradient norms efficiently.

To compute the LNP-components from Equation 24, we use the current training batch for dataset batch AA. For dataset batch BB, we use a fixed validation set of 160 samples, from which we draw a batch of 32 samples for each LNP computation within a window. Using the analysis from Appendix B.1, this setup results in an estimated computational overhead of approximately 27%27\% during training.

For the linear probe experiments, we use (i) the final model checkpoints obtained after training on SimpleStories and (ii) randomly initialized models as backbones. We then freeze the backbone and train a linear classifier on top of the final-layer representations using SimpleStories. All other model and training (hyper-)parameters are kept the same as in the main training setup to ensure a fair comparison of the learned representations.

B.2.2 CIFAR-5M Next Pixel

The CIFAR-5M dataset is a collection of 6 million (5 M train and 1 M test) generated CIFAR-10-like images (Nakkiran et al., 2020). We convert the images into grayscale flattened sequences of 1024 pixels with values in {0,…,255}\{0,\ldots,255\} and use a vocabulary size of 256 tokens for the next-pixel prediction task. We train Llama 2 transformer models of varying sizes (102.6K, 229.7K, 381.4K, 1.1M, 2.3M, 5.2M, 12.5M parameters) on the next-pixel prediction task (Touvron et al., 2023). Model details are provided in Table 2.

We train each model for a single epoch using AdamW with weight decay 0.010.01, β1=0.9\beta_{1}=0.9, and β2=0.95\beta_{2}=0.95. We use learning rates (4e-2, 3e-2, 7e-3, 5e-3, 4e-3, 2e-3, 2e-3) for the different model sizes (in order of increasing size), selected via preliminary grid searches. We apply a linear learning-rate warmup over the first 100 steps. We use batch size 128, context length 1024 tokens, and train for a total of 42207 steps. Experiments are repeated for 3 random model initializations, preserving the data order across runs.

We measure the LNP-components across logarithmically spaced windows during training. Specifically, we use S=23S=23 windows, each spanning W=50W=50 training steps. Because we compute the LNP-components only once within overlapping windows, this results in a total of 752752 training steps with LNP measurements. We use M=10M=10 random vectors for the Hutchinson estimator to compute sample-wise gradient norms efficiently.

To compute the LNP-components from Equation 24, we use the current training batch for dataset batch AA. For dataset batch BB, we use a fixed validation set of 4096 samples, from which we draw a batch of 128 samples for each LNP computation within a window. Using the analysis from Appendix B.1, this setup results in an estimated computational overhead of approximately 39%39\% during training.

For the linear probe experiments, we use (i) the final model checkpoints obtained after training on CIFAR-5M and (ii) randomly initialized models as backbones. We then freeze the backbone and train a linear classifier on top of the final-layer representations using the CIFAR-5M next-pixel prediction task. All other model and training (hyper-)parameters are kept the same as in the main training setup to ensure a fair comparison of the learned representations.

B.2.3 CIFAR-5M Image Classification

The CIFAR-5M dataset is a collection of 6 million generated CIFAR-10-like images (Nakkiran et al., 2020). We use the RGB images with 32×3232\times 32 pixels for an image classification task with 10 classes.

We train Vision Transformer (ViT) models of varying sizes (546.2K, 1.8M, 9.4M parameters) on the image classification task (Dosovitskiy et al., 2020). Model details are provided in Table 3.

We train each model for 5 epochs using AdamW with weight decay 0.050.05, β1=0.9\beta_{1}=0.9, and β2=0.999\beta_{2}=0.999. We use learning rates (2.86e-4, 1.89e-4, 9.0e-5) for the different model sizes (in order of increasing size), selected via preliminary grid searches. We use batch size 128, image size 32×3232\times 32 with patch size 4, and train for a total of 211034211034 steps.

We measure the LNP-components across logarithmically spaced windows during training. Specifically, we use S=51S=51 windows, each spanning W=50W=50 training steps. Because we compute the LNP-components only once within overlapping windows, this results in a total of 25502550 training steps with LNP measurements. We do not use Hutchinson’s trace estimator here, as the output dimension is small (10 classes) and we can compute sample-wise gradient norms exactly without significant overhead.

To compute the LNP-components from Equation 24, we use the current training batch for dataset batch AA. For dataset batch BB, we use a fixed validation set of 600268600268 samples, from which we draw a batch of 128 samples for each LNP computation within a window.

Using the analysis from Appendix B.1, this setup results in an estimated computational overhead of approximately 27%27\% during training.

B.2.4 CIFAR-5M Image Classification under muP

To disentangle width from feature-learning intensity (see Appendix D.3 for the motivation), we replicate the CIFAR-5M classification experiments of Appendix B.2.3 under maximal-update parameterization (muP) (Yang et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2022). We use the same CIFAR-5M dataset as in the standard runs (Appendix B.2.3).

We train Vision Transformer models under muP at the sizes in Table 4.

We apply muP following Yang et al. (2021); Yang et al. (2022) with base width dbase=192d_{\mathrm{base}}=192 and base learning rate ηbase=1.57​e-4\eta_{\mathrm{base}}=1.57\text{e-4}, tuned via a grid search at dbased_{\mathrm{base}}; all other hyperparameters are identical to the standard-parameterization runs (Appendix B.2.3). This also applies to the LNP measurement setup.

B.2.5 Random Feature Model Details

This setup is designed to validate the theoretical predictions in Equation 11 by creating a controlled environment where the LNP-components follow analytically tractable scaling behavior.

Data Generation.

We generate synthetic Gaussian data 𝐗∈ℝn×d\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} with n=10000n=10000 samples and input dimension d=128d=128. The data covariance matrix 𝚺=diag​(𝝁)\boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\text{diag}(\boldsymbol{\mu}) is diagonal with eigenvalues following a power-law decay: μk∝k−β\mu_{k}\propto k^{-\beta} for k=1,…,dk=1,\ldots,d, where β∈[1.0,3.0]\beta\in[1.0,3.0] controls the spectral decay rate. We normalize eigenvalues such that ∑k=1dμk=d\sum_{k=1}^{d}\mu_{k}=d. Each sample is generated as 𝐱i=𝐳i⊙𝝁\mathbf{x}_{i}=\mathbf{z}_{i}\odot\sqrt{\boldsymbol{\mu}}, where 𝐳i∼𝒩⁡(0,𝐈d)\mathbf{z}_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I}_{d}) and ⊙\odot denotes element-wise multiplication, yielding 𝐱i∼𝒩⁡(0,𝚺)\mathbf{x}_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}).

Student Architecture.

We employ a random feature model (RFM) with m=5000m=5000 hidden units and frozen first-layer weights trained via squared loss:

f𝐜​(𝐱)=1m​∑j=1mcj⋅σ⁡(𝐰j⊤​𝐱),f_{\mathbf{c}}(\mathbf{x})=\frac{1}{\sqrt{m}}\sum_{j=1}^{m}c_{j}\cdot\sigma(\mathbf{w}_{j}^{\top}\mathbf{x}), (53)

where 𝐖=[𝐰1,…,𝐰m]⊤∈ℝm×d\mathbf{W}=[\mathbf{w}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{w}_{m}]^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d} is the frozen projection matrix with entries Wj​i∼𝒩⁡(0,d−1)W_{ji}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,d^{-1}), σ​(⋅)=2⋅ReLU​(⋅)\sigma(\cdot)=\sqrt{2}\cdot\text{ReLU}(\cdot) is the variance-preserving ReLU activation, and 𝐜∈ℝm\mathbf{c}\in\mathbb{R}^{m} are trainable readout weights initialized at zero.

RKHS-Realizable Teacher.

The teacher function is constructed to lie exactly within the student’s reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS):

f∗​(𝐱)=1m​∑j=1mcj∗⋅σ⁡(𝐰j⊤​𝐱),f^{*}(\mathbf{x})=\frac{1}{\sqrt{m}}\sum_{j=1}^{m}c^{*}_{j}\cdot\sigma(\mathbf{w}_{j}^{\top}\mathbf{x}), (54)

where crucially, {𝐰j}j=1m\{\mathbf{w}_{j}\}_{j=1}^{m} are the same frozen projection vectors used by the student model, ensuring equal capacity and eliminating approximation errors that would arise from teacher-student capacity mismatch. The teacher coefficients are drawn as 𝐜∗∼𝒩⁡(0,𝐈m)\mathbf{c}^{*}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I}_{m}).

This construction ensures realizability: the target function f∗f^{*} is exactly representable within the function class of the student. Both models share the same feature map ϕ⁡(𝐱)=1m​[σ⁡(𝐰1⊤​𝐱),…,σ⁡(𝐰m⊤​𝐱)]⊤∈ℝm\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x})=\frac{1}{\sqrt{m}}[\sigma(\mathbf{w}_{1}^{\top}\mathbf{x}),\ldots,\sigma(\mathbf{w}_{m}^{\top}\mathbf{x})]^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{m}, and thus inhabit the same RKHS with kernel k⁡(𝐱,𝐱′)=ϕ​(𝐱)⊤​ϕ​(𝐱′)k(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})=\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x})^{\top}\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}^{\prime}). With this normalization, k⁡(𝐱,𝐱′)→K⁡(𝐱,𝐱′)k(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}^{\prime})\to K(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}^{\prime}) as m→∞m\to\infty, where KK is the population kernel of Appendix A.4.

Evaluation Protocol.

Labels are generated as 𝐲~=f∗​(𝐗)\tilde{\mathbf{y}}=f^{*}(\mathbf{X}) and normalized to unit variance: 𝐲=(𝐲~−𝐲~¯)/std​(𝐲~)\mathbf{y}=(\tilde{\mathbf{y}}-\bar{\tilde{\mathbf{y}}})/\text{std}(\tilde{\mathbf{y}}). We evaluate the model at initialization (before any training) to isolate the effect of the data spectrum and kernel structure. We compute the LNP-components with respect to the squared loss ℒ⁡(𝐜)=12​n​‖𝐲−𝚽​𝐜‖22\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{c})=\frac{1}{2n}\|\mathbf{y}-\boldsymbol{\Phi}\mathbf{c}\|_{2}^{2}, where 𝚽=[ϕ⁡(𝐱1),…,ϕ⁡(𝐱n)]⊤∈ℝn×m\boldsymbol{\Phi}=[\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_{1}),\ldots,\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_{n})]^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m} is the feature matrix with the zero-initialized readout layer. Each experiment is repeated across 100 random seeds (varying 𝐖\mathbf{W}, 𝐜∗\mathbf{c}^{*}, and 𝐗\mathbf{X}) to estimate the expected scaling behavior of χnet\chi_{\text{net}}, χloss\chi_{\text{loss}}, and χpos\chi_{\text{pos}} as a function of β\beta.

Appendix C Evaluation Details

C.1 Data Processing and Visualization

Loss Curve Smoothing.

The training loss values shown in Figure 1 are smoothed using an exponential moving average (EMA) with a smoothing factor of 0.1 for visualization purposes (McKinney, 2010). This reduces noise while preserving the overall trends in the loss dynamics.

LNP-Component Visualization.

The LNP-components displayed in Figures 1 and 5 are computed over the measurement windows specified in Section B.2. For Figure 1, we plot the full dynamics without averaging for the first 40 training steps to capture the initial behavior. After this point, we plot the average value computed over windows of 50 steps to provide a clearer view of the longer-term trends.

Handling Overfitting in Linear Probes.

For the linear probe experiments discussed in Section 5 and presented in Figure 4, we observe that models tend to overfit in later training stages. This overfitting leads to a reduction in the spectral position χpos\chi_{\text{pos}} that can obscure the natural reduction caused by learning smaller eigenvalue modes. To mitigate this effect, we apply the following strategy: from each measurement window, we select only the top 10% of spectral position values. Since this filtering is applied uniformly across all models, it does not introduce bias in the comparative analysis. Specifically, Equation 12 is evaluated by computing the ratio

χpos​(random)χpos​(pre-trained)=⟨χpostop 10%​(random)⟩τ>0.9​t⟨χpostop 10%​(pre-trained)⟩τ>0.9​t,\frac{\chi_{\text{pos}}(\text{random})}{\chi_{\text{pos}}(\text{pre-trained})}=\frac{\langle\chi_{\text{pos}}^{\text{top 10\%}}(\text{random})\rangle_{\tau>0.9t}}{\langle\chi_{\text{pos}}^{\text{top 10\%}}(\text{pre-trained})\rangle_{\tau>0.9t}}\,, (55)

where τ\tau denotes the normalized training time (ranging from 0 to 1) and ⟨⋅⟩\langle\cdot\rangle represents averaging over the selected data points within the specified time windows.

Appendix D Supplementary Experimental Results

D.1 Test Loss Scaling

This section provides the test loss scaling curves corresponding to the training loss results shown in Figure 1 (top). Figure 7 demonstrates that the scaling laws observed for training loss extend to test performance: test loss follows similar power-law relationships with model size for both SimpleStories (left) and CIFAR-5M next-pixel prediction (right). The power-law fits show comparable exponents and R2R^{2} values to those observed for training loss, confirming that larger models achieve better generalization performance and that the scaling behavior is not limited to fitting the training data.

D.2 Compute-Optimal Data/Model Trade-Off

The main paper presents scaling experiments along the model-size axis under a fixed single-epoch training recipe (Appendices B.2.1 and B.2.2). Here we examine how spectral position responds to a different slicing: at a fixed total compute budget, how does the choice between a larger model with less data and a smaller model with more data affect test loss and χpos\chi_{\text{pos}}?

Figure 8 traces these isocompute curves: test loss (left) and spectral position (right) as a function of model size at fixed FLOP budgets, on SimpleStories (top) and CIFAR-5M (bottom). Each color-coded curve corresponds to a single compute budget; points along a curve correspond to models of different sizes trained with that budget.

The qualitative behavior of χpos\chi_{\text{pos}} tracks that of test loss across both datasets: along each isocompute curve, χpos\chi_{\text{pos}} moves with the loss as the data/model ratio shifts. The two axes play complementary roles in spectral descent: more data provides more gradient steps for χpos\chi_{\text{pos}} to migrate into the spectral tail, while larger models lower the floor that χpos\chi_{\text{pos}} can ultimately reach (Section 4). At a fixed compute budget, χpos\chi_{\text{pos}} and loss therefore respond to the data/model trade-off in tandem: both reflect the same balance between training time and capacity.

D.3 Vision Transformer Classification: Standard and muP Parameterization

Beyond the language and next-pixel-prediction settings of the main text, we evaluate spectral reach on CIFAR-5M image classification with Vision Transformers (Appendix B.2.3). The standard-parameterization panel of Figure 9 (left) shows that the spectral-position phenomenon generalizes to vision classification: training loss decreases with model size, spectral position decreases throughout training, and larger ViTs reach lower χpos\chi_{\text{pos}} values.

Under standard parameterization, however, width and feature-learning intensity are entangled: changing model width also changes the rate at which representations evolve during training. The scale ordering observed in the main text could in principle be driven by either factor. muP (Yang et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2022) resolves this entanglement by rescaling weight initializations, learning rates, and (where applicable) attention temperatures so that feature-learning intensity is held constant across widths. If the ordering of spectral reach across model sizes persists under muP, it must be attributable to model capacity rather than width-dependent feature-learning intensity.

The muP panel of Figure 9 (right) shows that the ordering is indeed preserved: larger ViTs continue to reach lower χpos\chi_{\text{pos}} values. We conclude that the scale ordering reported in Section 4 is capacity-driven, not intensity-driven. Setup details for the muP runs are provided in Appendix B.2.4.

D.4 Dynamics of all LNP-Components

The main paper focuses on the dynamics of spectral position χpos\chi_{\text{pos}} (Section 4) and the gradient-magnitude scale χnet\chi_{\text{net}} (Section 5). Here we report the dynamics of all three LNP-components, χloss\chi_{\text{loss}}, χnet\chi_{\text{net}}, and χpos\chi_{\text{pos}}, as well as the product χnet⋅χpos\chi_{\text{net}}\cdot\chi_{\text{pos}}, for all model sizes on both SimpleStories (Figure 10) and CIFAR-5M next-pixel prediction (Figure 11).

Loss-magnitude dynamics.

By definition, χloss=‖∇fℒ‖22\chi_{\text{loss}}=\|\nabla_{f}\mathcal{L}\|_{2}^{2} depends only on the loss function and the current prediction errors, so it should mirror the loss curve up to model-independent factors. The top-left panels of both figures confirm this: χloss\chi_{\text{loss}} tracks the loss closely across all model sizes throughout training (compare to the top panels of Figure 1).

Spectral position decrease versus network-magnitude increase.

Because χnet=Tr​(Θ)\chi_{\text{net}}=\text{Tr}(\Theta) grows during training in feature-learning models, one might worry that the observed decrease in χpos\chi_{\text{pos}} is a passive consequence of trace inflation: as the kernel trace increases, the normalized spectral position would have to compensate. The bottom-right panels of Figures 10 and 11 rule out this explanation. The product χnet⋅χpos\chi_{\text{net}}\cdot\chi_{\text{pos}} more closely resembles χpos\chi_{\text{pos}} (bottom left) than χnet\chi_{\text{net}} (top right), indicating that the χpos\chi_{\text{pos}} decrease substantially exceeds the χnet\chi_{\text{net}} increase. A compensation between the two would produce an approximately constant product, which the data rule out. This is consistent with the direction-of-causality argument in Section 6, in which spectral bias drives the χpos\chi_{\text{pos}} decrease and the χnet\chi_{\text{net}} increase is its secondary, complementary response.

D.5 Explicit eNTK Eigendecomposition

The decomposition χpos=∑kγk2​pk\chi_{\text{pos}}=\sum_{k}\gamma_{k}^{2}\,p_{k} (Section 3) implies that a decrease in χpos\chi_{\text{pos}} over training corresponds, mathematically, to a shift of the projection coefficients γk2\gamma_{k}^{2} toward smaller normalized eigenvalues pkp_{k}. Here we verify this shift empirically by directly computing γk2\gamma_{k}^{2} and pkp_{k} from an explicit eNTK eigendecomposition.

To make the eNTK tractable, we evaluate it on a reduced output space: a single SimpleStories sample with K=40K=40 vocabulary indices and S=256S=256 token positions, on the 3.83.8M-parameter Llama model from the main experiments. We compare the spectra at initialization and after training.

Figure 12 reports the eigenvalue distribution pkp_{k}, the squared projection coefficients γk2\gamma_{k}^{2}, and their product γk2​pk\gamma_{k}^{2}\,p_{k} at the two checkpoints. After training, γk2\gamma_{k}^{2} is softly reweighted toward smaller eigenvalues, consistent with the mathematical prediction. The effect is moderate because of the constrained setup: the eNTK here is computed over roughly 6000×6000{\times} fewer tokens than in the main experiments, which compresses the spectral statistics toward the bulk of the distribution and reduces the separation between dominant and subordinate modes. We expect the shift to be substantially more pronounced at the scales used in the main analysis, where the full eNTK eigendecomposition is computationally infeasible.
